body.x: A small clinic with no dedicated phone staff misses calls over lunch, at night and on holidays. Each missed call can be a lost appointment, and the staff who do answer lose time to repetitive calls, booking changes and reminders that could go to patients.

WiseAI Co., Ltd., a medical AI operations platform company based at Pangyo Inno Valley in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province, built its business around that problem. Led by CEO Hyungseok Song, the company will take part in FIX 2026 and was named a winner in the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards. It says it has three goals at the show.

According to WiseAI, small hospitals and clinics make up a substantial share of Korean medical institutions and handle a large volume of repetitive work, such as phone inquiries, booking changes, visit reminders and recall calls, without staff to spare. In its own description, Song solves the problem of hospitals losing patients by missing calls, and his job is to let even small clinics respond to patients around the clock and manage return visits. The company's answer is AiU, an AI medical care platform that supports clinic booking, consultation and post-care. The company says AiU integrates inbound and outbound AI Call, a KakaoTalk AI chatbot, clinic-specific AI Pages, agent handoff, call recording, summarization and analytics, and identification and follow-up of patients who have not returned.

At the core of AiU is WaiGPT, which WiseAI describes as its proprietary inference engine. It combines a pattern-based reasoning engine with large language models (LLMs) and is trained on about 16 billion data points, with about 400 million added every month, the company says. It also integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI agents, in-house SIP telephony and robotic process automation (RPA) and optical character recognition (OCR). WiseAI says that lets AiU read and control a clinic's existing electronic medical record (EMR) screens and enter or change bookings automatically, without separate API partnerships or replacing the EMR.

WiseAI lists four strengths for the exhibit. First, AiU links seven stages in one engine: patient acquisition, inbound response, booking confirmation, EMR recording, outbound recall, agent operations and performance management. Second, clinics can adopt it with their existing EMR; WiseAI says it has integrated with more than 40 EMR and customer relationship management (CRM) systems and can support a new EMR within one to two weeks. Third, WaiGPT identifies intent even in typos and colloquial speech and generates answers from treatment history, care plans and clinic information, and the company says answers with an inference score below 70% and unanswered questions are retrained continuously. Fourth, its outbound functions identify patients who have dropped out of care and run purpose-specific calls that adapt to patient responses, with Visual AI Call, which pairs voice with on-screen guidance, scenario editing and automatic result logging. Support for 10 languages is meant to help clinics serve international patients.

The company reports results as well. As of the end of June 2026, AiU was deployed at about 700 medical institutions in 10 specialties, including dentistry, plastic surgery, health screening, dermatology, ophthalmology, Korean medicine and psychiatry, ranging from large clinics in the Seoul metropolitan area to dental and Korean medicine clinics in other regions. In evaluations by accredited external institutions, the company says, AiU averaged 93.17% accuracy for AI Call, 95.5% for AI Page and 95% for AI model classification, and call response success rates at adopting clinics rose from 71.5% to as high as 98.75%. WiseAI says it began with SSAM, an on-premise AI consultation solution, converted it into subscription software as a service (SaaS), and started with DentOn for dental clinics before moving into 10 specialties. It holds 32 registered patents, six pending applications and 11 certifications, and received a TI-1 rating in the NICE technology assessment, according to the company.

On financials, WiseAI says revenue grew about 13-fold, from KRW 0.8 billion in 2021 to KRW 10.4 billion in 2025, and that it has raised more than KRW 20 billion in Series A and B rounds. It was named a Baby Unicorn 200 company in 2023, selected for Baby Unicorn Plus in 2024 and listed in Forbes Korea's "Korea AI 50" in 2025. In the public sector, the company says it leads the 2026 AI Application Rapid Commercialization Program, piloting a chronic disease management model that combines an AI call center, wearables and remote consultation in medically underserved areas, including Baengnyeong Hospital and Ganghwa Hospital. Its core customers are dental clinics and specialty clinics with one to three physicians and no dedicated call center, especially dentistry, plastic surgery, dermatology and ophthalmology, where phone bookings are common and recalls and treatment-plan management bear directly on revenue. Abroad, it names small dental clinics in the U.S. and Japan as its first targets.

The company's goals at the exhibition are to present an AI operations model proven in Korean clinics, demonstrating the full flow from an inquiry received by AI Call or chatbot to a booking written automatically to the EMR and follow-up messages to patients who have not returned. It also wants to find overseas partners and buyers, including EMR and healthcare IT companies, distributors and provider networks for joint PoCs and sales partnerships, and to explore uses beyond healthcare in commerce, franchising, recruiting and public services, with local governments and public agencies for access to care.

WiseAI has recorded exports to Japan: USD 87,160 in 2022. It is working with a local Japanese EMR company to adapt AiU to local clinic operations and notes that Japan, like Korea, has a high share of small clinics that take bookings mainly by phone. It has no exports to the U.S. or the U.K. yet. In the U.S., it has signed memoranda of understanding (MOUs) with two dental clinics and is preparing deployment; in the U.K., it is pursuing a PoC through a local entity. Its priority markets are the U.S., Japan and the U.K. In the U.S., it cites high labor costs and heavy booking, recall and insurance inquiry workloads, and hopes to use its dental MOUs as first references and partner with dental EMR vendors, dental service organizations (DSOs) and healthcare IT distributors. In Japan, it points to many small clinics, an aging population and growing staffing shortages. It describes the U.K. as its gateway to Europe and says it is interested in working with medical tourism companies in Asia. Its approach is phased: validate performance within a controlled scope, then expand to AI Call, EMR integration and outbound recall, and scale through local partners once it has proven references.

WiseAI lists five challenges abroad. The first is privacy and health data rules in each country, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) in the U.S., UK GDPR in the U.K. and the Act on the Protection of Personal Information in Japan. The second is that EMR ecosystems differ by country, so securing local EMR partners and test environments remains a challenge. The third is that telecom infrastructure and numbering systems differ, so AI Call must comply with local carrier integration, caller ID and call-recording notice rules. The fourth is that building local references and trust takes time. The fifth is that local operations and support need staff and early-stage funding. The company says regulatory consulting, partner matching, PoC funding and overseas exhibition support would help.

Its plan has three directions. In Korea, it will improve AiU using operating data from about 700 institutions, apply specialty-specific learning and caching databases to similar institutions, strengthen performance management so clinics can see how AI activity turns into bookings and visits, and refine its C1, C2 and C3 subscription plans and usage-based pricing. Overseas, it will follow a "validate small, scale wide" strategy: expanding the Japanese EMR partnership and adding distributors, validating results with its U.S. dental clinics before moving through dental EMR vendors and DSOs, and using the U.K. PoC as a foothold in Europe. It also plans to turn its chronic care pilot in underserved regions into a standard model for other local governments and public hospitals, expand services that help people access benefits they are eligible for, and apply its booking, inquiry and guidance technology to commerce, franchising and recruiting with partners.

Now in its third year, FIX 2026 (Future Innovation Technology Expo) is a future-industry exhibition that connects innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It runs from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO in Daegu. Under the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," the exhibition shares industry trends and core technologies through AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by experts from Korea and abroad, and networking programs.
